whyItExists.problem: Images and media overflow their containers on small screens. Fixed-width layouts break. Videos lose their aspect ratio when resized.
whyItExists.solution: Responsive design combines fluid layouts, viewport meta, flexible images, and aspect-ratio control to create designs that work on every screen without JavaScript.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every project should be responsive. Over 60% of web traffic comes from mobile devices.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Internal tools used only on desktop can sometimes prioritise desktop experience — but even then, fluid layouts are usually worth the small extra effort.

explainModes.beginner: Responsive design means your page looks good on a phone, tablet, and desktop. You combine flexible widths, images that shrink to fit, and media queries to change layout at different screen sizes.
explainModes.simple: Key techniques: (1) Add the viewport meta tag to HTML. (2) Make images fluid with max-width: 100%. (3) Use % or fr for column widths. (4) Use media queries to change column count at breakpoints.
explainModes.standard: Responsive design is a philosophy: start mobile, use fluid units, add breakpoints only when the layout breaks. object-fit controls how images fill their box. aspect-ratio enforces consistent proportions. Container queries (modern) enable component-level responsiveness.
explainModes.technical: The viewport meta tag disables the default mobile browser zoom-out behaviour. Without it, a 1000px-wide page is shrunk to fit a 375px screen, making text tiny. max-width: 100% on img prevents overflow. object-fit: cover fills the box without distortion. The aspect-ratio property creates intrinsic ratios without the old padding-top hack.
explainModes.deepDive: Container queries (@container) are the next evolution: styles respond to a parent element's size rather than the viewport. A card component can change its layout based on its container width — making it truly reusable in sidebars, modals, or main content. Combine with the :has() pseudo-class for parent-aware conditional styling without JavaScript.

questions.question: What does object-fit: cover do?
options: Stretches the image to fill the box, distorting it
Fills the box while maintaining aspect ratio, cropping the overflow
Fits the image inside the box with letterboxing
questions.explanation: object-fit: cover fills the entire box while maintaining the image's aspect ratio. Any parts that don't fit are cropped. It is the most common value for card thumbnails.

questions.question: Why is the viewport meta tag required for responsive design?
options: It loads the page faster on mobile
It prevents mobile browsers from scaling down the page to fit the desktop width
It sets the default font size
questions.explanation: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers assume the page is desktop-width and zoom it out to fit — making text tiny. The meta tag tells the browser the page is already mobile-optimised.

faq.q: What is the difference between max-width: 100% and width: 100%?
faq.a: width: 100% forces the element to always be exactly its container's width. max-width: 100% allows the element to be smaller but prevents it from exceeding the container — ideal for images that should never overflow but shouldn't be forced full-width.

Container queries (@container) let you apply styles based on a parent element's width rather than the viewport. A card component can change layout based on its container — so it works correctly in a sidebar (narrow) or in main content (wide).

examples: Instagram's image grid uses aspect-ratio: 1 with object-fit: cover for uniform square thumbnails
YouTube's video cards use aspect-ratio: 16/9 to maintain widescreen proportions at any width
GitHub's file grid on mobile stacks to a single column using auto-fill minmax
